# Qualcomm Bets $14 Billion on Cracking Nvidia's AI Monopoly With RISC-V and an Open Compiler

Qualcomm confirmed Wednesday morning that it is acquiring Modular — the AI software startup whose Mojo programming language and MAX inference engine let developers run AI models across chips from Nvidia, AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm without rewriting their code — in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $3.92 billion, based on Qualcomm's Tuesday closing price. The announcement landed at Qualcomm's Investor Day, hours after the company also disclosed it expects to begin shipping custom silicon to a leading hyperscaler before the end of 2026.Alongside the confirmed Modular deal, Qualcomm remains in reported talks to acquire Tenstorrent — the AI chip startup built on the open RISC-V instruction set architecture and led by celebrated chip architect Jim Keller — at a valuation of between $8 billion and $10 billion, according to a June 15 report by The Information confirmed as a reported development by Reuters. That deal has not been announced; Qualcomm says it does not comment on rumors.Taken together, the two deals — the Modular acquisition confirmed today and the Tenstorrent talks still in progress — would commit more than $14 billion to a single strategic goal: making it possible for cloud providers and enterprise buyers to run AI workloads on hardware that does not come from Nvidia. Today's Investor Day is the first opportunity for CEO Cristiano Amon to lay out a formal data center revenue roadmap, with the Modular announcement as its opening act.Why Two Deals Are Needed to Challenge One CompanyNvidia's dominance in AI infrastructure rests on two supports that reinforce each other. The first is its GPU hardware, which remains the default choice for training large AI models. The second is CUDA, the parallel computing platform Nvidia has been building since 2006 that gives developers a unified programming environment for its chips. Approximately 4 million developers now work within the CUDA ecosystem, surrounded by decades of accumulated libraries, compiler tooling, and pre-optimized frameworks. Code written for CUDA does not run cleanly on a rival chip: migrating a workload to AMD, Intel, or Qualcomm silicon typically requires significant rewrites, which is why most customers stay on Nvidia even when alternative hardware is cheaper or faster for their specific workload.That software lock-in is precisely why Qualcomm needs Modular alongside Tenstorrent. Tenstorrent provides a different chip architecture designed to be more efficient than a GPU for the inference workloads that now dominate AI spending. Modular provides the compiler layer that makes that architecture accessible to developers who would otherwise face the cost and disruption of leaving CUDA. Together, they address the two reasons every previous Nvidia challenger has failed: not the chip, but the ecosystem.Modular co-founder and CEO Chris Lattner said in a statement that the acquisition gives his company the scale to advance its mission. "Joining Qualcomm gives us the scale and platform reach to accelerate that mission," Lattner said. "Together, we can make AI development more accessible and performant for developers." Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon framed the move as a structural bet on the direction of AI infrastructure. "As agentic AI scales across data centers and edge environments, the industry is moving toward disaggregated, multi-vendor architectures that demand a more open and modern software foundation," Amon said in a statement.What Tenstorrent Actually Built: How the Tensix Architecture WorksTenstorrent's Blackhole chip, which reached general availability on April 28, 2026, is built around the company's Tensix core architecture — a design that takes a fundamentally different approach to AI computation than the GPU parallelism Nvidia has refined over two decades.Each Tensix core contains five RISC-V processors — called "baby" cores internally — alongside local static RAM, a matrix engine for tensor operations, a vector engine for element-wise operations, and two routers that connect the core to the chip's internal mesh network. Of the five baby cores per Tensix unit, one handles moving data into the core, one handles moving data out, and three drive the compute engines. The Blackhole chip packs 120 of these Tensix cores alongside 16 larger RISC-V processor cores capable of running a full Linux operating system, all interconnected via a network-on-chip mesh. The chip delivers 664 TFLOPS of BF16 performance, carries 32GB of GDDR6 memory at 512GB per second bandwidth, and is built on TSMC's 6-nanometer process.The architecture's efficiency claim for inference workloads comes from this tile-based design. A conventional GPU hides memory latency by keeping thousands of simultaneous compute threads occupied — a strategy that works well for large training runs where data flows in large, predictable batches. For inference, where a single user request involves far fewer simultaneous operations, many of those threads sit idle while the chip waits for data from external memory, wasting both power and cost. Tenstorrent's Tensix cores each carry their own pool of on-chip SRAM. When model weights fit within that distributed local memory, the chip avoids the slow external DRAM accesses that drive GPU inference costs.The tradeoff is real. Developers must explicitly manage which data sits in which core's local SRAM and when it moves across the network — more demanding to program than writing a CUDA kernel. For chip-to-chip scaling, Blackhole uses standard 400 Gigabit Ethernet rather than Nvidia's proprietary NVLink interconnect, with four QSFP-DD ports providing 800Gbps of connectivity each. Standard Ethernet is more interoperable and cheaper to deploy in mixed-vendor environments, though its bandwidth density trails NVLink in the largest training clusters — a workload Tenstorrent is not primarily targeting.Tenstorrent has also built an open-source software stack called TT-Metalium, available under a permissive MIT license and supporting model deployment through PyTorch, JAX, and ONNX. This is the direct counterpart to CUDA — a programming environment for Tensix hardware that does not require a licensing relationship with Nvidia. As of mid-2026, it supports a growing range of large language models and video generation workloads but does not yet cover the full breadth of CUDA's library ecosystem. That gap is precisely what a Modular integration is positioned to narrow.What Modular Brings to the StackModular was founded in 2022 by Chris Lattner and Tim Davis. Lattner created the LLVM compiler infrastructure that underlies most modern programming language toolchains, the Swift language Apple uses across its platforms, and was a former Tesla Autopilot software executive. The company's Mojo language and MAX inference engine are designed to run the same AI model code on chips from different vendors without hardware-specific rewrites — the same platform today supports NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple Silicon GPUs as well as Intel, AMD, and ARM CPUs.The strategic value for Qualcomm is direct: a developer who adopts Modular's toolchain can move workloads between hardware vendors without the switching cost that makes CUDA so sticky. If Qualcomm can package Tenstorrent's Tensix silicon with Modular's hardware-agnostic inference layer, the standard objection to Nvidia alternatives — "we would have to rewrite everything" — becomes substantially weaker.Modular last raised $250 million in September 2025 at a $1.6 billion valuation. Today's $3.92 billion acquisition price reflects how quickly inference-software companies have been revalued. Nvidia itself struck a reported roughly $20 billion licensing agreement for assets from inference startup Groq, signaling that the software layer sitting between AI models and chips has become as strategically contested as the chips themselves.The Modular deal closes in the second half of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. Qualcomm will issue up to 19.2 million shares of common stock to Modular's equity holders in a private placement.Who Jim Keller Is, and Why the Tenstorrent Talks MatterJim Keller is the CEO of Tenstorrent and one of the most consequential chip architects of the past three decades. His design work spans the AMD K8 microarchitecture that introduced the Athlon 64, the Apple A4 and A5 processors that powered the iPhone 4 and the original iPad, AMD's Zen microarchitecture that ended Intel's dominance in server processors, and Tesla's Full Self-Driving computer. He joined Intel in 2018 and departed in 2020 before his work there reached production, and has led Tenstorrent since late 2020, becoming CEO in January 2023.Tenstorrent's team includes chip architects recruited from Apple's M-series program, AMD's Zen group, Intel, and Tesla. The company's Ascalon RISC-V CPU core — a separate product line from the Tensix AI accelerator, aimed at server and infrastructure applications — is a 64-bit out-of-order superscalar design that Tenstorrent claims places it in direct competition with ARM's Neoverse server cores. IP licensees already include LG and Hyundai; partners include Japan's Leading-edge Semiconductor Technology Center and BOS Semiconductors in Korea, which developed an automotive AI chiplet using Tenstorrent's technology.Analysts have flagged Keller's career pattern as the reported acquisition's principal risk. Keller has spent roughly two to four years at each major employer — AMD, Apple, Tesla, Intel — moving on before the products he designed reached market. Whether milestone-based earnout structures in an acquisition could extend that engagement through a full product execution cycle is a question the reported price does not yet answer.Intel was also reportedly interested in Tenstorrent as an acquisition target, according to a Bloomberg report from May 2026, which introduced competitive bidding dynamics into the valuation.What Qualcomm Already Has — and What the Acquisitions CompleteQualcomm is not arriving at the data center without a foundation. The company introduced its Dragonfly brand for data center AI inference chips at Computex 2026 and announced that its AI 200 accelerator — built on its Hexagon neural processing unit technology with direct liquid cooling and up to 768GB of LPDDR memory — is on track for initial customer shipments in 2026. A custom silicon product for a leading hyperscaler, which CEO Cristiano Amon identified on the company's second-quarter earnings call without naming the customer, is also expected to begin shipping before year-end. The most recent quarter showed handset revenue down 13 percent year over year, with automotive revenue up 38 percent and IoT up 9 percent.What Qualcomm's existing portfolio has lacked is a credible open-architecture AI accelerator with a demonstrated developer community and a shipping product. The December 2025 acquisition of Ventana Micro Systems provided a RISC-V server CPU design for compute nodes. The $2.4 billion Alphawave Semi acquisition supplied high-speed SerDes interconnect and optical connectivity IP for moving data across AI clusters. Tenstorrent would add the inference accelerator layer, and Modular would add the software layer that makes the entire stack usable without CUDA. The Dragonfly brand announced at Computex is the commercial packaging that wraps all of it.Analysts covering Qualcomm have projected that the company could announce data center revenue targets of more than $3 billion for fiscal year 2027, scaling to $35 billion by fiscal year 2031 — though those are analyst estimates, not company guidance. What will be confirmed at today's Investor Day is Qualcomm's formal framing of its data center ambitions, with the Modular acquisition as the first announced piece of that architecture.What Has Not Been SettledA Tenstorrent acquisition at the reported scale will require scrutiny. A semiconductor transaction of this size involving data center AI assets would typically require review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States on national security grounds and by the Federal Trade Commission on competition grounds. China's State Administration for Market Regulation launched a separate antitrust probe into Qualcomm in October 2025, targeting the company's acquisition of Israeli automotive chip designer Autotalks. That investigation remains unresolved. China generates a substantial portion of Qualcomm's global revenue, and enforcement at the maximum statutory rate would be a material event.The deeper unanswered question is whether the software ecosystem can follow the hardware. Intel's Gaudi accelerator has been in enterprise channels for years with substantial backing and has not moved at scale, in large part because the software layer that makes non-Nvidia silicon practically usable for developers never materialized quickly enough. The coherence of Qualcomm's reported twin-deal structure — hardware from Tenstorrent, software from Modular — suggests the company has identified the right problem. Whether it can deliver the answer is what the next several years will determine.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is Tenstorrent and how does its chip architecture differ from Nvidia GPUs?Tenstorrent is a Canadian AI chip company, founded in 2016 and led by CEO Jim Keller, that builds AI accelerators on the RISC-V open instruction set architecture. Tenstorrent's software stack, TT-Metalium, is open-source under a permissive MIT license, in contrast to Nvidia's proprietary CUDA platform.What did Qualcomm confirm at its Investor Day on June 24, 2026?Qualcomm confirmed its acquisition of Modular, an AI software startup, in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $3.92 billion based on Qualcomm's Tuesday closing share price. Qualcomm will issue up to 19.2 million shares of common stock to Modular's equity holders. The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. Qualcomm has also been reported to be in separate discussions to acquire AI chip startup Tenstorrent for between $8 billion and $10 billion, but that deal has not been confirmed.Why does Qualcomm need both a chip company and a software company to challenge Nvidia?Nvidia's AI market position rests on two distinct advantages: GPU hardware optimized for parallel compute, and the CUDA software ecosystem that has accumulated two decades of developer tooling, libraries, and roughly 4 million developers. A hardware alternative alone does not eliminate the switching cost that keeps customers on Nvidia, because existing AI code is written for CUDA and requires significant rewrites to run on different silicon. Modular's Mojo language and MAX inference engine let developers write AI code that runs across multiple chip vendors without hardware-specific rewrites, removing the primary practical barrier to adopting Tenstorrent's hardware — or any non-Nvidia silicon — for inference workloads.What is RISC-V and why does it matter for the AI chip market?RISC-V is a free, open-standard instruction set architecture developed at the University of California, Berkeley in 2010, based on reduced instruction set computing principles.
